topic: AI app reports private diary to police

headline: AI diary leads to felony charge after company reports private entries to police
summary: A woman's private diary, kept in a third-party AI app, was reported to police by the company. She now faces a felony charge.
details: A woman used a commercial AI assistant as a diary, writing private thoughts. The company scanned this content, flagged it, and reported her to law enforcement. She now faces a felony charge, with her private thoughts becoming state's evidence.
This incident highlights the critical difference between data custody and ownership. When you put data into someone else's product, you gain convenience like sync and search, but you give up custody.

Users do not control who inside a company reads their data, what automated systems scan for, or which government jurisdiction the company answers to. A subpoena, reporting obligation, or internal safety policy can dictate what happens to your data.
The uncomfortable lesson is that a policy you don't write, applied to data you don't hold, can produce an outcome you never consented to. You will not get a vote in these decisions.
Data hosted on a platform is not inert; it fuels models, ranking systems, and analytics. It can become a compliance artifact or a liability that the platform manages on its own terms.

Ultimately, data you don't hold is data that can be used against you. Unlike a bad vendor, this is not something you can easily migrate away from after the fact, emphasizing the importance of owning your data layer.

topic: Amazon profiles users with 'flat buttocks' data
headline_marked: [[Amazon knows you have 'flat buttocks']] and other intimate details based on your purchases
headline: Amazon knows you have 'flat buttocks' and other intimate details based on your purchases
summary: A viral Threads post revealed how Amazon infers surprisingly personal details from shopping habits, including physical attributes. Find out what the retail giant thinks about you.
details: Amazon collects data based on your purchases, inferring details like owning cats or being prone to breakouts. However, a Threads user recently discovered Amazon's assumptions can get uncomfortably intimate, including the claim she "has flat buttocks."

The user, @fangirlinmegan, shared her shock on Threads, noting that while the assumption was based on her purchase of "butt scrunch leggings," it was still a jarring revelation. Her post quickly garnered over a million views, prompting many others to check their own Amazon profiles.

To find this information on desktop, hover over "Hello, [your name]" in the upper right corner, then click "Account." Under "Ordering and shopping preferences," select "Your Shopping preferences." Scroll to the bottom and click the blue hyperlinked option that says "Manage your information."

On the mobile app, navigate to the hamburger icon from the bottom menu bar. From there, go to Account > Shopping preferences > About you. This section will reveal the various assumptions Amazon has made about your interests and characteristics.

Other users have found Amazon correctly inferred interests like photography, collectible card games, being "invested in the Apple ecosystem," or a penchant for "natural materials" and clothing that "prioritizes comfort." These insights highlight the extensive nature of Amazon's data collection.

The incident underscores how closely tech companies pay attention to user behavior on their platforms. While some inferences might be benign or even flattering, the depth of this surveillance can be alarming, revealing how much personal data is being gathered.
